ready3_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The graphs of the polar curves $r = 2 + \cos \theta$ and $r = -3 \cos \theta$ are shown on the graph below. The curves intersect when $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\theta = \frac{4\pi}{3}$. Region $R$ is in the second quadrant, bordered by each curve and the y-axis.
Set up but do not evaluate a formula to find the area of $R$.
ready3_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: The graphs of the polar curves $r = 2 + \cos \theta$ and $r = -3 \cos \theta$ are shown on the graph below. The curves intersect when $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\theta = \frac{4\pi}{3}$. Region $R$ is in the second quadrant, bordered by each curve and the y-axis. Set up but do not evaluate a formula to find the area of $R$.
ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure there are rectangular coordinate axes and a grid; on the left there is a circular curve mainly located to the left of the y-axis, corresponding to the polar curve r=-3\cos\theta in the problem statement; on the right there is a larger limacon-shaped curve, labeled in the figure as r=2+\cos\theta. The two curves intersect near the upper left and lower left, and the region R is marked in the second quadrant, in the position between the two curves. Then reason: The problem statement gives that the angles corresponding to the intersection points of the two curves are \theta=\frac{2\pi}{3} and \theta=\frac{4\pi}{3}, so use these two angles as the limits of integration. To determine the outer radius and inner radius, take the representative angle \theta=\pi in the interval: r=-3\cos\pi=3, while r=2+\cos\pi=1, so r=-3\cos\theta is the outer radius and r=2+\cos\theta is the inner radius. Thus according to the area formula between two curves in polar coordinates, the area can be set as A=\frac12\int_{\frac{2\pi}{3}}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}}\left[(-3\cos\theta)^2-(2+\cos\theta)^2\right]d\theta, and calculation is not needed.
